rs12.reasoning: 'Spectre-gray', 'dregs', 'desolate' and 'weakening eye of day' all show decline. 'Crisp, invigorating' goes against the stanza's desolation.
The strings belong to 'broken lyres', which cannot be played. Line 6 is a visual image of stems 'scoring' the sky, and it says nothing about melody.
The stem asks what the metaphor is for. Crypt and death-lament turn the century's end into a funeral. Reading it as literal description ignores that it is a metaphor at all.
Leaning on the gate puts him outdoors. Line 8 puts everyone else indoors. No other option fits.
'Seemed ... as I' measures the world by his own mood, so he is projecting. The other options contradict the line.
A sudden song of 'joy illimited' breaks into the deathly scene. The other options misread its function.
'Aged, frail, gaunt, and small' stresses weakness, so the joy comes in spite of frailty. Nothing in the text says the bird is strong.
The bird flings 'his soul', not his body, and 'had chosen' marks a deliberate act. Reading it as literal flight is wrong.
'Shrunken hard and dry' set against 'full-hearted evensong' opposes feeling to lifelessness. The other options misread the contrast.
The final contrast is about knowing, 'he knew / And I was unaware', and the poem stresses the bird's frailty, not its physical strength. So the envy-of-strength option fails.
'I could think' frames the bird's knowledge as the speaker's guess. 'Confirming' a 'divine plan' overstates both the certainty and the content.
The poem ends on an unresolved gap between the bird's hope and the speaker's unawareness. The other options misread the ending.
Only line 25 addresses the lack of cause for the song. The other quotations are not about that claim.
'Nothing but despair' leaves out the thrush and the 'blessed Hope'. The keyed thesis covers the whole poem.

rs13.reasoning: This is a personification of the houses, which have 'brown imperturbable faces' and are 'conscious of decent lives.' That points to smug respectability. Nothing in the text says any resident literally spies from a window.

The narrator says it deadpan, right next to the detail that the money went to institutions and the furniture to his sister. That makes it quiet irony. 'Openly scornful' and 'hoarded wealth' have no support in the text.
The boy gives his reason outright: 'because its leaves were yellow.' That is a response to how the book looks, not to its plot.
The cold makes the boys' 'bodies glowed,' and this is set against the 'dark muddy lanes,' ashpits and 'dark dripping gardens.' Every distractor is contradicted by the text.
The light contrast picks her out as an idealized figure. The word 'only' rules out option 1, and nothing in the text supports options 2 or 3.

The stem asks about the contrast between the two boys. The brother treats her casually while the narrator stands silently 'looking at her.' The brother's reluctance belongs to one side only and misses the contrast.
Hiding so he 'could not be seen' while following her every morning is intent pursuit kept secret. The text never mentions guilt or shame.
In first person the girl is seen only from outside, through the boy's eyes. All the distractors are contradicted by the text.
'Foolish' describes his own blood, not the girl. It reads as an older narrator looking back ruefully, not with bitter contempt for her.
'Her image accompanied me even in places the most hostile to romance' carries her influence from the street into the market. None of the other options fits.
The chalice image makes his love a sacred charge, and the 'throng of foes' is the hostile world around it. 'Mainly fear' ignores the sacred image.
The admissions are about emotion he cannot understand ('could not tell why'). They ask the reader to recognize feeling the boy cannot name. Physical sensory overload misreads what he is admitting.
The boy is the harp, and her words and gestures make him resonate. 'Deliberately' adds an intention the text never gives her.
Only option 0 covers the whole passage: the religious imagery, the drab setting and the boy's devotion. The priest material takes up one paragraph and cannot support a thesis about the whole passage.
'Strange prayers and praises' applies religious language directly to the narrator's feelings for her. 'Litanies' describes the shop-boys' cries, not his infatuation.

rs15.reasoning: 'Any one can play accurately' makes his lack of skill sound like a refined choice, and Lane's polite refusal to listen undercuts him. The comic frame ('I keep science for Life') rules out reading him as a serious artist.
Lane's general remark about married households is a calm dodge of the implied charge that the servants drank the champagne. It is not a sincere expert verdict.
Calling his marriage 'a misunderstanding' with 'a young person' and adding 'I never think of it myself' is flat understatement, not earnest confession.
Algernon scolds Lane for lax views on marriage, then says he would 'try to forget the fact' of his own marriage. That is hypocrisy, not sincere concern about moral decay.
Only the reader sees the speech label 'JACK' next to the announced name 'Ernest.' On stage he is called only Ernest, so 'openly uses two names' has no support.
Algernon's pointed question about Shropshire and Jack's flustered 'Eh? Shropshire?' suggest Jack is hiding something. The distractors are contradicted by the text.
'One so young' refers to Algernon, not Jack. The joke lies in using grave moral language about a tea with cucumber sandwiches.
Algernon turns Jack's 'pleasure, pleasure!' back on him by calling a proposal 'business.' The other options misstate facts in the text.
Option 0 contradicts 'It is very romantic to be in love.' The line 'the very essence of romance is uncertainty' supports the key.
'You behave as if you were married to her already... You are not' directly supports the idea that Jack presumes a claim he has not yet won.
Algernon eats the sandwiches he forbids Jack to touch, so his 'devotion' to his aunt is only a pretext. That fits self-serving enforcement of the rules.

Lane is not morally superior: he drinks the champagne and brushes off his own marriage, and 'faithfully' overstates his loyalty. The key captures how the scene's inversions expose talk about marriage as self-interest.
